data.title: Delhi HC says restaurants, hotels cannot impose mandatory service charges
data.description:
The Delhi High Court on Thursday clarified that it had not granted any interim protection to restaurants and hotels against an earlier order prohibiting them from automatically collecting service charges from customers.
 
A Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma said no interim relief had been granted against the single judge's March 28, 2025, order.
 
The clarification came after Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, appearing for the Centre, pointed out that some restaurants continued to treat service charges as compulsory despite the High Court's earlier ruling.
 
Sharma submitted that the practice was contrary to the single judge's order, which upheld the Central Consumer Protection Authority's (CCPA) 2022 guidelines prohibiting hotels and restaurants from adding service charges to bills by default.
 
 
"Ball is in your court. It is for you to take action. We can't take action. Where is the interim relief? Where is the interim relief in their favour? We have not granted any interim prayer," Acting Chief Justice Sambre observed.
 
The Bench was hearing appeals filed by the National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI) and the Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Associations of India (FHRAI) challenging the single judge's decision. The court admitted the appeals for hearing.
 
The CCPA issued its guidelines in July 2022 after receiving complaints from consumers about restaurants adding service charges, typically ranging between 5 and 20 per cent, to food bills without their consent.
 
The NRAI and FHRAI challenged the guidelines, contending that service charges were a longstanding industry practice and were linked to employee compensation and labour arrangements.
 
However, the single judge found no material to establish that the charges directly benefited employees. The court held that payment of service charges must remain voluntary and that compelling customers to pay them amounted to an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
 
The ruling also upheld the CCPA's authority to regulate such practices and held that its guidelines were legally binding.
 
The single judge further restrained restaurants from using the term 'service charge' in a manner that could mislead consumers into believing it was a government-imposed levy. Establishments were asked to use alternative descriptions such as 'voluntary contribution' or 'staff welfare fund'.
 
Restaurants were also directed not to add such charges automatically to bills and to clearly inform customers that tipping was optional.
 
In its appeal, the NRAI has argued that service charges should not be treated as an unfair trade practice when their collection is disclosed on menus and at restaurant premises.
 
It has also contended that the practice is recognised in the hospitality industry and forms part of employee compensation under labour arrangements.
 
The association has questioned whether the dispute should be examined under labour law rather than consumer protection law. It has further challenged the CCPA's authority to regulate pricing structures that customers are informed of and accept while placing orders.

data.title: Behind every meme, a worry: What India's youth are really losing sleep over
data.description:
India is one of the world’s youngest countries, and its youth are growing up in uncertain times: prices keep climbing, jobs feel less secure, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work. Globally, 54 per cent of lower earners think AI will leave them behind, compared with 31 per cent of high earners. Scroll through their feeds and you’ll find reels and memes about all of it. But behind every meme is a real worry.
 
 
Red Lab’s (the consumer insights wing of Rediffusion) The Worry Report, based on seven major surveys across more than 100 countries, including Deloitte’s 2026 GenZ and Millennial Survey, attempts to identify them. They turn out to be ordinary concerns: rent, health, jobs, bills, parents, and the planet.
 
The money squeeze
 
For Indian youth, the anxiety starts with money. About 20 per cent of GenZ and 19 per cent of millennials name the cost of living as a top concern. On more concrete measures, India fares better than the world: 20 per cent of GenZ and 13 per cent of millennials struggle to meet their monthly expenses, compared with 34 per cent globally for both groups. Financial insecurity tells a similar story, affecting 29 per cent of GenZ and 18 per cent of millennials in India, against 45 per cent and 44 per cent, respectively, worldwide.
 
 
The pressure shows up in decisions, not just bank balances. While 37 per cent of GenZ and 20 per cent of millennials say they cannot afford a home (compared with 51 per cent and 40 per cent globally), 76 per cent of GenZ and 62 per cent of millennials say housing costs influence their career choices. The question is no longer just which job pays well, but which city’s rent they can afford. Meanwhile, 54 per cent of GenZ and 44 per cent of millennials have postponed a major life decision because of money.
 
Getting in, holding on
 
GenZ and millennials aren’t losing sleep over the same things. GenZ is worried about getting in. Unemployment is its top concern, cited by 27 per cent (against 22 per cent of millennials), while long working hours are its biggest workplace stressor, cited by 53 per cent.
 
Millennials, meanwhile, are worried about holding on: 50 per cent say they do not feel supported by their leaders, their top workplace stressor, while 45 per cent say they do not have enough hours to finish their work.
 
Planet and the power bill
 
Climate change weighs more heavily on millennials. It is a top concern for 34 per cent of India’s millennials, compared with 23 per cent of GenZ, and causes considerable stress for 38 per cent of millennials. Yet the share naming the environment among their top three life concerns has slipped to 23 per cent from 26 per cent in September 2025.
 
Part of the reason may be the electricity bill. Worldwide, 74 per cent worry about rising energy prices. Half would prioritise low energy prices even if emissions increased. That isn’t necessarily indifference to the planet; people simply dread an unexpectedly high bill.
 
A world on edge
 
Global politics also weighs heavily on young people’s minds. Worldwide, 69 per cent say the world has become worse over the past year, reflecting pessimism rather than a sense of personal danger. Ending wars is the top priority in 21 of the 34 countries surveyed and ranks among the top two priorities in 33. Yet people haven’t given up on one another: 57 per cent want their country to cooperate with others on global problems, even if that means compromise, up from 55 per cent in 2025. About eight in 10 would be more supportive of such cooperation if it delivered visible results. Confidence in the major powers remains thin, with only 39 per cent comfortable with the US playing a leading global role and 37 per cent with China doing so.
 
Who to believe
 
Worldwide, 65 per cent believe foreign actors deliberately flood their media with falsehoods to inflame divisions, up from 54 per cent in 2021. In India, the figure is 70 per cent.
 
People at the dinner table
 
Indian youth worry about others as much as they do about themselves. Globally, 48 per cent name health among their top three concerns, with the figure rising from 40 per cent among GenZ to 59 per cent among Baby Boomers. In India, however, family health is GenZ’s biggest stressor, cited by 44 per cent, compared with 37 per cent of millennials.
 
Worried, not broken
 
The data isn’t all bleak, though. As many as 76 per cent of GenZ and 83 per cent of millennials in India rate their mental well-being as good or extremely good. However, 24 per cent of GenZ and 18 per cent of millennials say they feel stressed all or most of the time. A further 73 per cent and 81 per cent, respectively, say their employers take mental health seriously, up from 70 per cent and 78 per cent in 2025.
 
What stands out is how modest the ask is. Indian youth aren’t demanding a revolution. They want rent they can manage, a job that lasts, a bill that doesn’t spike, and a future they can plan around. In short, stability.

data.title: Policy, tax incentives needed to boost financial savings: DIPAM secretary
data.description:
India needs to use policy, regulatory and tax incentives to channel household savings toward financial assets and to bring more individuals into the formal financial system to meet the country’s growing investment requirements, Arunish Chawla, secretary of the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (Dipam), said on Thursday.
 
“Historically, the distribution of our household savings has not entirely been towards financial savings. A significant amount of it has gone into real estate, gold and other valuables,” he said at the CII Financing Summit 2026. He added that savings and investment are the growth engines of the economy and household savings will be critical to financing India’s development ambitions.
 
 
“The question is how we can incentivise the behaviour through policy, regulation and tax incentives, so that ordinary Indians, working Indians, saving Indians, become part of our formalised financial economy and help finance the needs of Viksit Bharat in both the public and private sectors,” he said.
 
Chawla highlighted the growing participation of households in financial markets, pointing to the expansion in demat accounts and mutual fund investments. The number of demat accounts had increased more than sixfold, from around 36 million in 2019 to 250 million in October 2026. Mutual fund assets under management had risen from ₹15 trillion in 2016 to ₹84 trillion last month.
 
“This is the great democratisation of our capital markets. This is a watershed moment and this is what we need to work on,” he said.
 
He also flagged the need to deepen India’s bond and fixed-income markets to ensure a better balance between equity and debt financing. Banks alone would not be sufficient to meet the economy’s long-term financing requirements, making market-based financing and greater mobilisation of pension funds important.
 
Another challenge, he said, was ensuring access to capital across the life cycle of businesses, from startup and growth capital to expansion, monetisation and reinvention.
 
Chawla also called for greater use of public-private partnerships and capital markets to finance infrastructure, including through infrastructure investment trusts (Invits), which can help monetise infrastructure and underutilised land assets.

data.title: SC questions use of Article 32 by homebuyers in stalled housing projects
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Thursday questioned whether homebuyers should approach it directly under Article 32 of the Constitution to resolve disputes arising from stalled housing projects, instead of raising their grievances before the appropriate lower courts.
 
A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, along with Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana, observed that the Supreme Court could not be expected to adjudicate every dispute between homebuyers and builders.
 
“Under Article 32, how many such matters are we going to resolve? Every dispute against a builder, every failed project, will end up here. How are we going to resolve it?” CJI Kant remarked during the hearing.
 
 
The observations came during proceedings on a petition filed by homebuyers in a stalled housing project in Sonipat, Haryana. They had approached the apex court seeking protection from recovery proceedings initiated by the State Bank of India (SBI) over loans taken to purchase flats in the Krishna Housing Scheme in Sector 14.
 
The homebuyers had entered into a tripartite arrangement with the developer and SBI to finance the under-construction flats. Under the agreement, the bank was required to release loan instalments in phases, depending on the progress of construction.
 
However, the developer allegedly failed to complete the project and was subsequently admitted into insolvency proceedings before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
 
The petitioners told the court that they had neither received possession of their flats nor the refunds assured under the insolvency proceedings. Despite this, SBI had initiated recovery proceedings against them before a commercial court in Saket, Delhi.
 
They sought an interim stay on the recovery action and requested that their petition be tagged with another pending matter concerning loans extended to builders.
 
CJI Kant questioned why the homebuyers had not pursued their objections before the commercial court, where the recovery proceedings were already pending.
 
“You have filed a commercial suit? It is pending before the civil court. Raise all your objections there,” he told the petitioners' counsel.
 
The lawyer submitted that the buyers had already raised their objections before the commercial court, but recovery proceedings were continuing. He also alleged that the developer had failed to pay the six-monthly instalments of refunds promised under the NCLT proceedings.
 
The Supreme Court subsequently directed the commercial court to examine the homebuyers' objections before allowing the bank to proceed with recovery.
 
In its order, the Bench noted that SBI appeared to have disbursed loans to the developer without corresponding progress in construction.
 
It said the commercial court must first examine the contractual arrangement between the bank and the builder, including whether the loan amounts had been released in accordance with the tripartite agreement.
 
“In our considered opinion, it is the duty of the court first to determine the nexus between the builder and the bank authorities and to see whether the bank disbursed the loan amount to the builder strictly in terms of the tripartite agreement,” the court said.
 
The Bench directed that no coercive recovery measures be taken against the homebuyers until the commercial court determines whether they were actually in default.

data.title: Trideep Bhattacharya quits Edelweiss AMC as CIO-Equities after five years
data.description:
Trideep Bhattacharya has quit Edelweiss Asset Management as its president and chief investment officer (CIO)-Equities after a five-year stint with the firm, sources said. As CIO, he oversaw equity assets worth around ₹45,000 crore while co-managing 10 schemes, including the fund house's largest active equity scheme — Edelweiss Midcap Fund — which has assets under management (AUM) of about ₹20,000 crore.
 
The midcap fund, sources said, will now be managed by Sahil Shah, who has returned to the fund house after leaving in 2024. He was associated with Edelweiss Asset Management for over 15 years and was the co-fund manager of the midcap fund at the time of leaving the company.
 
 
Prior to returning to Edelweiss, Shah was the fund manager-AIF at Kotak Asset Management.
 
Edelweiss MF is yet to announce a new CIO-Equities. Bhattacharya, who had resigned in October, will remain with the firm for about two more months.

data.title: PFRDA weighs higher distributor commissions, changes to pension fund mix
data.description:
The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) Chairman, S Ramann, said on Thursday that the regulator was examining ways to increase distributor commissions and make pension products more attractive as payouts to distributors remain significantly lower than those in the mutual fund industry.
 
He was addressing the Gatekeepers of Governance 2026 event in Mumbai.
 
Despite increasing the pool of commissions available to distributors by 2.5 times, payouts in the pension sector were still around a fifth of the levels offered by mutual funds, Ramann said. The low commissions have been one reason pension products have not gained wider acceptance, he added.
 
 
The regulator was also assessing the cost of distributor commissions for subscribers over the long term, given that pension investments could remain in place for 30 to 50 years. The impact of commissions needed to be assessed over the entire investment period, including their compounding effect, while balancing distributor incentives against the overall cost to subscribers.
 
“We actually have a bit of an inverse problem as compared to the insurance industry where money on the table for the distributors is so abysmally low that it is one of the reasons why probably the pension product never really went out in a big way. So, even after having increased the total sort of distributable commissions that lie on the table two and a half times, we’re still one-fifth the commission’s level which is available in the mutual fund industry,” he said.
 
Alongside distribution, PFRDA was reviewing the investment allocation of pension funds to improve long-term returns, including the scope for higher exposure to growth assets and alternative investment funds (AIFs).
 
The regulator has set up two expert committees to examine asset allocation: one headed by former State Bank of India Chairman Dinesh Khara and the other by investment expert Narayan Ramachandran, who has experience in the mutual fund industry. The committees have provided inputs on whether pension savings are invested in suitable asset classes to generate better returns for retirement payouts.
 
Ramann pointed to Australia’s superannuation system, where 72 per cent of the pension corpus remains invested in growth assets and the remaining 28 per cent in fixed-income instruments. Nearly half of the allocation to growth assets remains in unlisted investments.
 
India’s pension system remains risk-averse, with relatively little capital flowing into greenfield projects and startups. To widen investment opportunities, the National Pension System (NPS) has started its own fund of funds to invest in AIFs, allowing pension savings to participate in a diversified pool of investments.
 
PFRDA is also examining the possibility of introducing a market-based guarantee mechanism for pension payouts to private-sector subscribers. A committee headed by Sahu is studying the proposal, though such guarantees would involve an additional cost for subscribers.
 
Ramann said the regulator would examine the proposal and consider introducing changes gradually.

data.title: NHB seeks separate affordable housing loan norms for smaller cities: MD
data.description:
The National Housing Bank (NHB) is considering approaching the Department of Financial Services (DFS) to seek a separate classification for affordable housing loans in Tier II and III cities, proposing that loans up to ₹15 lakh be included in that category, said Sanjay Shukla, managing director, NHB, on Thursday.
 
He said housing affordability varies depending on the location and questioned whether the ₹25 lakh benchmark was appropriate across different cities.
 
Speaking at the CII Financing Summit, Shukla said, "Whether twenty-five lakh is sacrosanct figure because what is there in Mumbai may not be right for Bhusawal, may not be right for Aurangabad. So again we have approached with DFS and we want some classification further. Like in tier two, tier three cities, loan up to fifteen lakh should be classified as an affordable housing loan."
  
He also said NHB is working to deepen the residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) market to help housing finance companies diversify funding sources and reduce dependence on bank borrowings.
 
The NHB-backed RMBS development company has completed two transactions, while a third transaction is underway and is expected to be completed within a month, with the institution targeting another 20 such transactions over the next year.
 
Housing loans are typically long-term products of 15-20 years, while housing finance companies and non-banking financial companies largely depend on bank funding with tenures of five to seven years. Securitisation can help address this asset-liability mismatch, Shukla said.
 
He said NHB had disbursed ₹66,000 crore under the Affordable Housing Fund, supporting 6.2 lakh dwelling units.
 
Under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban) 2.0, NHB has signed agreements with 254 institutions and sanctioned nearly ₹438 crore for 1.1 lakh beneficiaries, he said.
 
Earlier, under the PMAY-Urban Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS), NHB disbursed ₹49,000 crore, benefiting 21 lakh beneficiaries.
 
He urged stakeholders to focus on three priorities to expand affordable housing finance and also said that lenders should extend credit to underserved borrowers, particularly those with informal incomes, by combining co-lending, refinancing and interest subsidies rather than treating them as separate initiatives.
 
As the industry expects a 25-50 basis point rate hike, he said that housing finance companies should build funding structures that can withstand interest-rate cycles through securitisation, housing bonds and diversified sources of capital.
 
Further, lenders and policymakers should measure housing credit growth through parameters such as loan ticket size, income segments and geographical distribution, rather than focusing only on aggregate lending growth, he added.

data.title: Boba Bhai raises $18 million in Series B funding to expand store network
data.description:
Boba Bhai, India’s largest bubble tea and Korean street food brand, has raised $18 million in Series B funding with participation from Left Lane Capital and BIG Capital, alongside existing investors, including Titan Capital. The round brings US-based Left Lane Capital on board as a new investor, while BIG Capital is increasing its investment in the company. The fresh capital will be used to accelerate Boba Bhai’s store expansion across India and support the launch and scale-up of new brands under Boba Bhai Ventures.
 
“Young Indian consumers are far more willing to experiment with global food formats today, but novelty alone does not build a lasting food brand. What matters is whether you can deliver the same product and experience consistently as you scale,” said Dhruv Kohli, founder, Boba Bhai. “Over the last three years, we have learnt a great deal about what travels across markets, what consumers come back for and what it takes to make a store work.”
 
 
Three years since its launch in October 2023, the company has expanded to 120 stores across India and is serving more than 300,000 orders every month across its physical and digital channels.
 
The Series B follows Boba Bhai’s ₹40 crore funding round announced in March 2026, which was led by 8i Ventures, Titan Capital Winners Fund and Global Growth Capital, with participation from BIG Capital and prominent angel investors.
 
Boba Bhai has built its growth around a combination of bubble tea, Korean street food and fusion offerings. It sells across physical retail, food-delivery platforms and quick commerce.
 
The infrastructure and capabilities built while scaling Boba Bhai will also form the foundation for the company’s multi-brand strategy under Boba Bhai Ventures. Rather than building each new consumer food brand from scratch, the company plans to use its existing capabilities across operations, supply chain, teams and digital distribution to launch and scale new concepts more efficiently.
 
Left Lane Capital’s investment follows its evaluation of India’s QSR market, with Boba Bhai’s growth, store-level profitability and payback periods among the key factors behind its investment decision. The US-based consumer investment firm has backed food and consumer businesses across global markets, including Blank Street Coffee and 7th Street Burger. Boba Bhai is the fourth company in India to be backed by Left Lane Capital.
 
“We have tracked Boba Bhai's growth for over two years and have been consistently impressed by how Dhruv has built the business. Boba Bhai stands out for its capital efficiency, its ability to quickly launch new concepts tuned to the local palate, and its relentless execution in delivering differentiated offerings for the Indian consumer,” said Arjun Kapur, principal, Left Lane Capital.
 
BIG Capital, which participated in Boba Bhai’s previous funding round, is increasing its investment through the Series B as the company moves into its next phase of growth.
 
“What gives us confidence to invest further is the team’s ability to grow while staying disciplined on the fundamentals of the business,” said Preetinder Singh Panjrath, partner, BIG Capital.

data.title: Delhi HC stays Lokpal proceedings against Defence Secretary Rajesh Singh
data.description:
The Delhi High Court has put on hold proceedings initiated by the Lokpal against Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh over a corruption complaint relating to promotions at the National Productivity Council (NPC).
 
A Bench of Justice Subramonium Prasad and Justice Renu Bhatnagar said the proceedings would remain stayed until the next hearing in January. The court also sought responses from the Lokpal and the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Singh's petition challenging the proceedings.
 
Senior Advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the Defence Secretary, argued that the CBI had already found no criminality in the allegations, but the Lokpal had chosen to proceed despite the agency's findings.
 
 
He submitted that the Lokpal was required to independently form an opinion on the existence of a prima facie case and seek an explanation from his client before proceeding further. That exercise, he argued, had not been carried out.
 
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the CBI, told the court that the matter might require closer examination.
 
Singh has challenged an October 26 order of the Lokpal directing a hearing against him under Section 20(3) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. He has also questioned a subsequent notice issued on October 28, besides an earlier order dated March 4, 2025, through which the Lokpal had assumed jurisdiction to entertain the complaint.
 
The petition states that the present proceedings stem from an earlier Lokpal order and notice issued in January 2025. Both were subsequently quashed by the High Court on November 28, 2024.
 
In that decision, the High Court had held that the Lokpal had not recorded the mandatory prima facie satisfaction regarding the commission of an offence of corruption. It had also observed that allegations merely bordering on corruption did not meet the statutory threshold for initiating further proceedings.
 
Singh has alleged that the Lokpal is attempting to revive the proceedings that were previously set aside by relying on documents introduced during the fresh hearing.
 
He has also contended that the complaint concerns administrative decisions involving service rules, selection procedures and promotions at the NPC, rather than any offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
 
At the time of the promotions under scrutiny, Singh was serving as Secretary of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) and was the ex-officio Chairman of the NPC's Governing Body. However, the promotions in question were made in March 2023, before he assumed charge of the department in April 2023, the petition states.
 
The plea further relies on a preliminary inquiry conducted by the CBI, which reportedly found the allegations against Singh to be unsubstantiated.
 
Singh has also questioned the decision to place the matter before the same seven-member Lokpal Bench that had earlier dealt with the complaint. He contends that the Bench had already expressed its views on the allegations, raising concerns about the principles of natural justice.

data.title: Rupee extends gains for fourth straight session on strong foreign inflows
data.description:
The Indian rupee appreciated for the fourth consecutive session on Thursday, supported by strong foreign portfolio inflows into domestic equities and a revival in overseas investment in government bonds. The domestic currency settled at 93.30 per US dollar, compared with its previous close of 93.45.
 
The rupee gained ground despite a relatively strong dollar, with softer crude oil prices and the return of foreign capital providing support. However, the strength of the greenback remains a key risk for the domestic currency. The dollar index, which measures the US currency against a basket of six major currencies, was down 0.1 per cent at 103.7 on Thursday after touching a high of 103.8. The index remained elevated following signals from the US Federal Reserve that further interest rate increases could be considered.
 
 
Minutes of the October meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) showed that almost all officials felt further rate hikes could be appropriate. Some members also indicated that an increase of more than 25 basis points (bps) could be considered in December. Fed Governor Christopher Waller also floated the possibility of a 50 bps hike.
 
Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) bought more than ₹88,000 crore worth of Indian equities in November so far, marking the highest monthly pace of inflows since November 2020. During the November 2020 buying phase, the Nifty rallied 12 per cent over three months and 30 per cent over 12 months.
 
The return of foreign investor interest is also extending to the debt market, which has witnessed a turnaround in inflows. After three consecutive months of net selling, overseas investors bought $1.1 billion worth of Indian government bonds in November.
 
The yield differential between Indian and US 10-year government bonds widened to 2.20 percentage points as of November 16 from 1.94 percentage points in September, improving the relative returns on Indian bonds for overseas investors. Foreign holdings of index-linked government securities also rose to nearly two-month highs.
 
ICICI Securities said the rupee broke out of its six-month consolidation range of 96.85-94.15, signalling a potential trend reversal.
 
"This bodes well for further appreciation in the rupee towards an implied target of the 91 per dollar mark eventually," the brokerage said in a report.
 
"Technically, the rupee has immediate support around 93.10-93.30, followed by 93.00. On the upside, 94.90-95.20 remains the next important resistance zone," said Amit Pabari, managing director at CR Forex.
